objectives: Trace lesion-case neuropsychology from Phineas Gage + Broca + Wernicke through H. M. + split-brain.
Survey standardized + flexible neuropsychological assessment (WAIS + Halstead-Reitan + Boston Process).
Apply cognitive-neuroscience methods (fMRI + ERP + TMS) + theory (Damasio + Phelps + Decety) to brain-behavior questions.

slides.title: Classic lesion cases that built neuropsychology
slides.body:
**Neuropsychology** + biological psychology study brain-behavior relationships. The discipline's central methodological move was — for two centuries — to use **brain damage as a natural experiment**, inferring function from selective deficits. The classic cases remain pedagogically central even as modern neuroimaging supplements + sometimes overturns the inferences.

**Phineas Gage** (1823-1860) — the most famous case in the history of neuropsychology. On 13 September 1848 a railroad-construction explosion drove a 3.5-foot tamping iron through his left cheek, behind the left eye, through the frontal lobes + out the top of the skull. Gage survived, walked + spoke within minutes, + lived another 12 years. His physician **John Martlyn Harlow** reported personality + behavioral changes (1848, 1868): 'no longer Gage' — impulsivity, profanity, difficulty with planning, social inappropriateness. The case suggested the **frontal lobes mediate executive + social-emotional regulation**. Modern reanalyses (Damasio + Damasio 1994 *Science*; Van Horn et al. 2012) reconstructed the lesion + supported the implication of ventromedial + dorsolateral PFC + their white-matter connections. Gage is the prototypical case of **acquired personality change after frontal damage** — a finding that re-emerged in Damasio's modern ventromedial PFC patients (E. V. R.; *Descartes' Error* 1994).

**Tan = Louis Leborgne, Broca's patient** — **Pierre Paul Broca** 1861 (Paris): a patient called 'Tan' (the only word he could say) was examined after death. Broca identified a lesion in the **left inferior frontal gyrus** (now Broca's area; BA 44/45). Broca's 1861 + 1865 papers — 'we speak with the left hemisphere' — established (a) localization of language + (b) cerebral lateralization. **Broca's aphasia**: non-fluent, agrammatic, effortful speech with relatively spared comprehension. Modern caveats: Broca's original brain (preserved in the Musée Dupuytren) shows damage well beyond the cortical region named after him; pure Broca's aphasia from purely cortical lesions is rare.

**Carl Wernicke** 1874: described a different aphasia — fluent but meaningless speech, impaired comprehension, **paraphasias** — with lesions to the left posterior superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke's area; BA 22). The Wernicke-Lichtheim model + later Wernicke-Geschwind model (1965) gave the classic neuroanatomy of language: Wernicke comprehension + Broca production connected via the arcuate fasciculus; conduction aphasia from arcuate lesions. Hickok + Poeppel (2007) dual-stream model later updated this.

**Henry Molaison ('H. M.')** (1926-2008) — the most studied human in neuroscience. In 1953 William Beecher Scoville performed a bilateral medial-temporal-lobe resection (including most of the hippocampus + amygdala + adjacent cortex) to treat intractable epilepsy. The seizures improved; H. M. developed **profound anterograde amnesia** — inability to form new declarative + episodic memories — with relatively intact working memory + procedural learning + premorbid memories.
- **Brenda Milner + William Scoville** (1957) classic paper in *J. Neurology, Neurosurgery + Psychiatry*: established the hippocampus as central to declarative-memory formation.
- Milner + Corkin + later Suzanne Corkin documented H. M.'s preserved mirror-tracing learning (procedural memory) despite no recollection of doing the task — the **double dissociation** that proved multiple memory systems.
- H. M. founded the modern psychology + neuroscience of memory; the H. M. → episodic + declarative + non-declarative distinction (Tulving + Squire) is built on his case.
- H. M.'s brain was sliced postmortem (Annese et al. 2014, *Nature Communications*); 'Permanent Present Tense' (Corkin 2013) is the definitive biography.

**Roger Sperry split-brain studies** — Sperry + Gazzaniga + colleagues from the 1960s; **Nobel 1981**. Patients with intractable epilepsy underwent **corpus callosotomy** to prevent interhemispheric seizure spread. Behavioral testing with stimuli presented selectively to one visual hemifield (thus one hemisphere) revealed dramatic findings:
- The left hemisphere is verbal + linguistic for most right-handers; the right hemisphere is mute in these patients but performs visuospatial + face-processing + emotion tasks.
- Each hemisphere can act independently — patients sometimes have the **alien-hand sign** or report inability to verbalize what their left hand 'knows'.
- Gazzaniga developed the **interpreter** hypothesis (1980s+): the left hemisphere confabulates coherent narratives to explain right-hemisphere-driven behavior — a striking demonstration that the unified self is a constructive achievement.
These studies revolutionized views of consciousness, hemispheric specialization, + the unity of mind.

**Other classical cases**:
- **Clive Wearing**: severe anterograde + retrograde amnesia from herpes encephalitis; intact musical knowledge + procedural performance.
- **K. F.** (Shallice + Warrington 1970): severely impaired short-term memory with intact long-term; evidence against the strict Atkinson-Shiffrin serial model.
- **Capgras delusion + prosopagnosia**: face-recognition + face-emotion dissociations.
- **Anosognosia** (Babinski 1914): denial of impairment after right-hemisphere stroke.

slides.title: Modern neuropsychological assessment
slides.body:
**Clinical neuropsychology** uses standardized + flexible test batteries to characterize cognitive profiles in patients with brain injury, dementia, developmental disorders, psychiatric conditions, + medico-legal contexts.

**General intellectual functioning — David Wechsler scales**:
- **WAIS** (Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale; current edition **WAIS-5** 2024; previously WAIS-IV 2008). The most widely used adult IQ test. Four indices: Verbal Comprehension, Perceptual Reasoning, Working Memory, Processing Speed (WAIS-IV) — restructured in WAIS-5. Composite Full-Scale IQ. Standardized + age-corrected; deviation IQ (M = 100, SD = 15).
- **WISC-V** for children (2014) + **WPPSI-IV** for preschool.
- **WMS** (Wechsler Memory Scale; current WMS-IV) — paired with WAIS to assess memory.
Wechsler's contribution: deviation IQ + age-graded norms + multifactorial structure that maps onto modern factor-analytic intelligence theory (Carroll's three-stratum, CHC). IQ scores correlate substantially with general mental ability (Spearman *g*) + predict educational + occupational + health outcomes (Deary, Lubinski, Plomin).

**Halstead-Reitan Battery** (Ward Halstead 1947; Ralph Reitan from the 1950s+): a **fixed comprehensive battery** of motor, sensory, attention, abstraction, memory tests including Category Test, Tactual Performance, Trail Making A + B, Speech Sounds Perception, Seashore Rhythm, finger-tapping, sensory perceptual exam. The Impairment Index (proportion of tests in the impaired range) is the summary score; Average Impairment Rating + General Neuropsychological Deficit Scale follow. Strengths: comprehensive + normed across age-sex-education; identifies global + lateralized + localized impairment; long evidence base. Weaknesses: lengthy (6-8 hr); not tightly tied to cognitive theory; less flexible for specific referral questions. Used in clinical + forensic settings.

**Boston Process Approach** — **Edith Kaplan** + colleagues (1980s+): a **flexible + hypothesis-driven** approach. Rather than running a fixed battery, the clinician constructs an individualized assessment based on the referral question + uses standardized tests but emphasizes **how** the patient performs (error analysis, strategy use, qualitative observation) as much as the final score. Boston Diagnostic Aphasia Examination, Boston Naming Test, Boston Stimulus Cards, Delis-Kaplan Executive Function System (D-KEFS — Dean Delis + colleagues). The Boston Process Approach contrasts with Halstead-Reitan's fixed-battery tradition + is closer to modern cognitive-neuropsychology practice.

**Specific domains + tools**:
- **Memory**: WMS, California Verbal Learning Test (CVLT-3), Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test, Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure, Wechsler Memory Scale.
- **Executive function**: D-KEFS, Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (Berg 1948; Heaton 1981 standardized), Stroop, Trail Making B, NIH EXAMINER, BRIEF.
- **Attention + processing speed**: Conners' Continuous Performance Test (CPT), digit-symbol coding, paced auditory serial-addition test (PASAT).
- **Language**: Boston Diagnostic Aphasia Examination, Western Aphasia Battery, Boston Naming Test, FAS verbal fluency.
- **Visuospatial**: Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure, Hooper Visual Organization Test, Judgment of Line Orientation (Benton).
- **Premorbid estimation**: National Adult Reading Test (NART), Test of Premorbid Functioning (TOPF); used to estimate prior IQ for comparison with current functioning.
- **Effort + validity**: Test of Memory Malingering (TOMM), Word Memory Test, Reliable Digit Span — essential for forensic + disability + post-concussion assessments.
- **Brief screening**: MMSE (Folstein 1975), MoCA (Nasreddine 2005 — more sensitive to mild cognitive impairment than MMSE).

**Use cases**:
- **Dementia + mild cognitive impairment** (Alzheimer + Lewy body + frontotemporal + vascular).
- **Traumatic brain injury** + post-concussion.
- **Epilepsy presurgical evaluation** (Wada test + fMRI).
- **Stroke** + multiple sclerosis + Parkinson + Huntington.
- **ADHD + learning disabilities + autism**.
- **Psychiatric differential** (depression-related vs neurodegenerative cognitive complaints).
- **Medico-legal**: malingering + capacity + forensic.

Standards: APA Division 40 (Clinical Neuropsychology); American Board of Clinical Neuropsychology; cross-cultural adaptation + norming is an active concern (most norms WEIRD-skewed).

slides.title: Cognitive neuroscience: fMRI, ERP, TMS + integrative theory
slides.body:
**Cognitive neuroscience** emerged in the 1990s from the merger of cognitive psychology + neuroscience + the availability of human neuroimaging. It complements lesion + animal work.

**Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI)** — Ogawa, Tank, Menon, Ellermann 1990; first human fMRI studies 1991-92 (Kwong, Belliveau, Ogawa). **BOLD signal** = Blood Oxygen Level Dependent contrast — deoxyhemoglobin is paramagnetic, oxyhemoglobin is not; local neural activity → increased blood flow → relative decrease in deoxyhemoglobin → increased MR signal. Spatial resolution ~1-3 mm; temporal resolution ~1-5 s (limited by hemodynamic response). Allows non-invasive whole-brain mapping during task performance + at rest (resting-state fMRI revealed the default mode network — Raichle, Greicius). Now the dominant human cognitive-neuroscience method, with caveats:
- BOLD is indirect (vascular, not neural).
- Statistical analysis is subtle — multiple-comparisons problem; Eklund et al. (2016) cluster-inference cautionary paper.
- Reverse inference: 'brain region X is active, therefore process Y' is invalid in many cases (Poldrack 2006, 2011).
- Reliability + replicability concerns; Marek et al. (2022) — many brain-wide association studies need thousands of subjects.

**Event-Related Potentials (ERP)** — averaged scalp EEG time-locked to a stimulus. Excellent temporal resolution (millisecond); modest spatial resolution. Workhorse components:
- **P1/N1**: early visual perception.
- **N170**: face-selective response (Bentin 1996); fusiform face area homologue.
- **N400** (Marta Kutas + Steven Hillyard 1980): semantic-incongruity component — large negativity to unexpected words in sentences.
- **P600**: syntactic anomalies + reanalysis.
- **Error-related negativity (ERN)** + **feedback-related negativity (FRN)**: action monitoring + reinforcement learning.
- **P300/P3b**: target detection + working-memory updating.

**MEG** (magnetoencephalography): MEG sensors detect tiny magnetic fields from neuronal currents; better source localization than EEG; combined with structural MRI gives spatio-temporal precision.

**Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS)** — Anthony Barker 1985: brief magnetic pulse over scalp induces cortical current. Single-pulse TMS can disrupt processing in a target region during a task ('virtual lesion' — Pascual-Leone); repetitive TMS can have longer effects + is clinically used for depression (FDA 2008). **TMS + fMRI** combinations test causal claims: knock out a region + observe consequences in distant regions.

**Transcranial Direct + Alternating Current Stimulation (tDCS, tACS)**: low-current scalp stimulation; effects modest + variable; replication concerns.

**Intracranial recording in humans**: epilepsy patients with implanted electrodes provide unique single-unit + LFP data (Itzhak Fried, Rodrigo Quian Quiroga — 'Jennifer Aniston neurons' in MTL coding specific concepts).

**Animal + invasive methods** (cross-ref P64-adjacent neuro paths): electrophysiology, optogenetics (Deisseroth, Boyden 2005 onward), chemogenetics (DREADDs), 2-photon calcium imaging, transgenic models, brain organoids. These provide mechanism + causal manipulation not possible in humans.

**Integrative cognitive-neuroscience theory**:

**Antonio Damasio** — **somatic markers + the social brain** (*Descartes' Error* 1994; *The Feeling of What Happens* 1999; *Self Comes to Mind* 2010):
- Vmpfc patients (E. V. R. + others) show preserved IQ but impaired social + financial + emotional decision-making.
- **Somatic Marker Hypothesis**: visceral + bodily feedback (somatic markers) tag options with affective value + guide decision; vmpfc integrates this; damage produces 'flat' decision-making by pure cognition alone.
- **Iowa Gambling Task** (Bechara, Damasio + colleagues 1994): a behavioral assay of intact somatic markers + intuition-driven choice; vmpfc patients fail to avoid disadvantageous decks even after learning the contingencies.
- Influence on philosophy of mind, embodied cognition, social-affective neuroscience.

**Elizabeth Phelps** — **emotion + memory** (NYU then Harvard; *Annual Review of Psychology* 2006 amygdala-hippocampal-PFC):
- Amygdala-hippocampal interactions modulate memory consolidation; emotional events are remembered better via amygdala-dependent modulation of hippocampal encoding + consolidation.
- **Fear conditioning** in humans (Phelps + LeDoux); reconsolidation + memory updating (Schiller + Phelps 2010): reactivating a fear memory + then updating during the reconsolidation window can attenuate it without extinction — translational implications for PTSD.
- Amygdala + race + implicit attitudes (Phelps 2000; cross-ref lesson 3).

**Jean Decety** — **social + affective neuroscience + empathy** (University of Chicago):
- Neural basis of empathy: shared representations between self + other (mirror-system + perception-action coupling) + perspective-taking + emotion regulation.
- *The Neurobiology of Empathy* (Decety + Ickes 2009); *Empathy: From Bench to Bedside* (Decety 2012).
- Pain empathy (Singer + Decety): observing another's pain activates affective-pain regions in the observer — the anterior insula + anterior cingulate.
- Developmental social neuroscience; moral development + judgment (Decety + Cowell).

**Other major frameworks**:
- **LeDoux dual-route fear** (low road via thalamus → amygdala vs high road via cortex); revised in *Anxious* (2015).
- **Predictive coding** (Friston; Rao + Ballard) — see lesson 8.
- **Default mode network** (Raichle 2001): a coherent network active at rest + implicated in self-referential + mind-wandering + autobiographical processing.
- **Triple network model** (Menon 2011): central executive + salience + default mode.
- **Embodied + grounded cognition** (Barsalou).
- **Reinforcement learning + dopamine** (Schultz, Dayan, Daw — see lesson 8).

Cognitive neuroscience supplements + sometimes corrects the lesion + cognitive-psychology heritage; modern programs integrate behavior + neuroimaging + computational models + clinical translation. The replication crisis hit fMRI especially hard + has driven larger samples + preregistration + open data (cross-ref lesson 8).

question.question: Reason through a memory-deficit case
question.goal: A 58-year-old presents with sudden inability to form new memories of conversations + recent events; she remembers her childhood + her name + can converse + use language fluently. Walk through the neuropsychological reasoning.

steps.prompt: What memory systems are intact + impaired?

acceptedAnswers: intact remote declarative + procedural + working memory; impaired anterograde episodic + likely anterograde semantic

steps.reveal: Intact: remote (premorbid) declarative memory (childhood, identity), procedural + working memory (conversation, language). Impaired: **anterograde episodic memory** (forming new memories of events) + likely anterograde semantic. The pattern resembles H. M. (Scoville + Milner 1957) — a hippocampal/medial-temporal-lobe (MTL) syndrome.

steps.prompt: What lesion location is most likely?
steps.reveal: Bilateral medial temporal lobe + especially the hippocampus + adjacent entorhinal + perirhinal + parahippocampal cortices. This is the H. M. (Scoville + Milner 1957) lesion. Squire's hierarchical taxonomy maps the bilateral MTL onto anterograde declarative memory formation + consolidation; intact remote memory implies preserved neocortical storage of consolidated memories.

steps.prompt: What etiologies could produce this in a 58-year-old?

acceptedAnswers: herpes simplex encephalitis + transient global amnesia + anoxic injury + early-onset Alzheimer + autoimmune (limbic) encephalitis + medial-temporal stroke

steps.reveal: Sudden onset: **herpes simplex encephalitis** (HSV-1 has tropism for MTL — Clive Wearing's etiology), **transient global amnesia** (TGA — recovers within 24 hr), **anoxic / hypoxic injury** (cardiac arrest, CO poisoning — hippocampal CA1 vulnerable), **medial-temporal stroke** (PCA territory), **autoimmune limbic encephalitis** (anti-NMDA, anti-LGI1, paraneoplastic), **Wernicke-Korsakoff** if there is concurrent thiamine deficiency. Subacute: early-onset Alzheimer disease. Workup: MRI with FLAIR + DWI, LP, EEG, autoimmune panel, vitamin B1, neuropsych testing.

acceptedAnswers: WMS-IV + CVLT-3 + Rey + WAIS for premorbid IQ + Boston Process + treat etiology + cognitive rehabilitation + caregiver support

steps.reveal: Assessment: **WMS-IV** for memory profile; **CVLT-3** + **Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test** for verbal learning; **Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure** for visual memory + organization; **WAIS-5** to estimate current IQ; **TOPF** for premorbid estimation; **Boston Naming + FAS** for language; **D-KEFS** for executive. Treatment: etiology-specific (acyclovir IV for HSV; thiamine for Wernicke-Korsakoff; immunotherapy for autoimmune; etc.). Cognitive rehabilitation (errorless learning, spaced retrieval, external aids); caregiver education; safety planning; longitudinal follow-up. The H. M. literature predicts persistent anterograde amnesia if MTL damage is extensive + bilateral; partial recovery if unilateral or partial.

question.question: Why is the **H. M. case** considered the most important single case in the history of neuropsychology?
options: Henry Molaison (1926-2008; 'H. M.') underwent bilateral medial-temporal-lobe resection in 1953 by William Beecher Scoville for intractable epilepsy. The seizures improved, but he developed profound + lasting **anterograde amnesia** with relatively preserved premorbid memory, intact working memory, + intact procedural learning (he learned mirror-tracing across sessions without any recollection of the prior sessions). **Brenda Milner + Scoville** 1957 paper in *J. Neurology, Neurosurgery + Psychiatry* established the **hippocampus + adjacent MTL as central to declarative-memory formation**. The case grounded the modern multiple-memory-systems framework: Tulving's episodic vs semantic (1972), Squire's declarative vs non-declarative — built on the H. M. dissociations. H. M. was studied continuously for >50 years (Suzanne Corkin); his brain was sectioned postmortem (Annese et al. 2014). The case anchors the field: the most cited neuroscience case, foundation of modern memory research, + a profound example of how careful single-case study can reshape an entire science.
question.explanation: H. M. (Henry Molaison) underwent bilateral MTL resection by Scoville in 1953; Scoville + Milner 1957 reported profound anterograde amnesia with preserved working + procedural memory. Established the hippocampus as central to declarative memory formation. Grounded Tulving's episodic-vs-semantic + Squire's declarative-vs-non-declarative taxonomies. Studied >50 years; brain sectioned postmortem (Annese 2014). The most consequential case in neuropsychology.

slides.workedSolution: H. M. (Molaison) underwent bilateral MTL resection (Scoville 1953). Scoville + Milner 1957 reported profound anterograde amnesia + preserved working + procedural memory. Established hippocampus + MTL as central to declarative-memory formation + grounded multiple-memory-systems taxonomy (Tulving, Squire). Most consequential single case in neuropsychology.

question.question: Designing a cognitive-neuroscience study post-replication-crisis
question.prompt: Your lab proposes an fMRI study of empathy in 30 adult participants, contrasting brain responses while observing a stranger in pain vs neutral images. You aim to test Decety + Singer's claim that the anterior insula + anterior cingulate cortex are engaged by pain empathy. A senior colleague warns that brain-wide-association studies need thousands of subjects (Marek et al. 2022 *Nature*); Eklund et al. (2016) cluster-inference critique applies; reverse-inference (Poldrack 2006) is a risk; + the replication crisis (lesson 8) has hit fMRI hardest. Drawing on (a) the methodological literature; (b) the available alternative methods (ERP N1/N2 + TMS over rTPJ + lesion patients with vmpfc damage + larger consortia like ABCD); + (c) the cost-benefit of a small study, write a study-design memo. Address how you would justify the N, what preregistration + region-of-interest choices, how you would interpret null vs positive results, + what role this small study could play in a wider research program.

question.question: In an ERP face-perception study, the **N170** component peaks at approximately 170 ms post-stimulus over occipitotemporal sites. If the participant's MRI head model places the source ~2 cm beneath the scalp + neural conduction in cortex is approximately 1 m/s for short-range axons, what is the conduction-delay component from source to scalp (in ms)? (Use $t = d / v$ with $d = 0.02 \text{ m}$ + $v = 1 \text{ m/s}$.)
question.hint: $t = d / v = 0.02 / 1 = 0.02 \text{ s} = 20 \text{ ms}$. The N170 latency (~170 ms) is dominated by stimulus processing + cortical computation, not conduction; this is why MEG + EEG temporal resolution can speak meaningfully to cognitive processes on the millisecond scale even with distributed sources.

question.prompt: In ≤140 words, trace neuropsychology from the classic lesion cases (Phineas Gage + Broca + Wernicke + H. M. + split-brain) through modern assessment (Wechsler + Halstead-Reitan + Boston Process) to cognitive neuroscience (fMRI + ERP + TMS) + theory (Damasio + Phelps + Decety).
question.rubric: Mentions: Phineas Gage (1848, Harlow 1848/1868; reanalyses Damasio 1994, Van Horn 2012) showed frontal lobes mediate executive + social-emotional regulation. Broca (1861) + Wernicke (1874) — left-hemisphere language lateralization; Broca's vs Wernicke's aphasia; Wernicke-Geschwind model. H. M. (Scoville + Milner 1957) — bilateral MTL → profound anterograde amnesia with intact procedural; founded multiple-memory-systems framework (Tulving + Squire). Sperry split-brain (Nobel 1981) — hemispheric specialization + Gazzaniga interpreter. Assessment: Wechsler scales (WAIS-5 + WMS) for IQ + memory; Halstead-Reitan fixed comprehensive battery; Boston Process flexible hypothesis-driven approach (Kaplan + Delis D-KEFS); specific tools per domain. Cognitive neuroscience: fMRI BOLD (Ogawa 1990; resting-state default mode); ERP components (N170 face, N400 semantic, P600 syntax; Kutas 1980); TMS virtual lesions; intracranial recording. Theory: Damasio somatic markers + Iowa Gambling + vmpfc patients; Phelps amygdala-hippocampal-PFC + fear reconsolidation; Decety empathy + perception-action + pain empathy + social neuroscience. Modern programs integrate behavior + imaging + computation + clinical translation under replication-aware standards (lesson 8).
